This module presents the Qur’an on its own terms. Here is how the Catholic Church speaks of Muslims — you can explore it or leave it.

The Second Vatican Council (Nostra Aetate 3) says the Church regards Muslims with esteem: they adore the one God, living and subsisting in Himself, merciful and all-powerful, Creator of heaven and earth. They revere Jesus as a prophet, though not as God, and honor Mary, his virgin mother, and at times call on her with devotion. They await the day of judgment.

The Catechism (841) adds that Muslims “together with us adore the one, merciful God.” Christians believe that the Word that the Qur’an calls “a word from Allah” (4:171) became flesh (John 1:14).

column7: Allah! There is no deity save Him, the Alive, the Eternal. Neither slumber nor sleep overtaketh Him. Unto Him belongeth whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is in the earth. Who is he that intercedeth with Him save by His leave? He knoweth that which is in front of them and that which is behind them, while they encompass nothing of His knowledge save what He will. His throne includeth the heavens and the earth, and He is never weary of preserving them. He is the Sublime, the Tremendous.

column4: Sanctissimum Rosarium
The oneness of God is the center of Islam: God has no partner, no equal, and nothing resembles Him (112).
Every surah but one opens with God’s names ar-Rahman, ar-Rahim — the Beneficent, the Merciful. Mercy is the name God has “prescribed for Himself” (6:12).
The five daily prayers turn the whole day toward God; prostration is the posture of complete surrender (islam).
Giving a portion of wealth to the poor purifies the giver and is one of the five pillars.
The Qur’an honors Jesus, son of Mary, as a great prophet and the Messiah, born of a virgin, called a word and a spirit from God (4:171), while denying that he is God’s son.
Mary is the only woman named in the Qur’an, and a surah bears her name (19). She is chosen and purified above the women of creation (3:42).
Belief in the Last Day and the resurrection of the body is a pillar of faith; every soul will see what it has done.
The Qur’an’s annunciation (3:42–47; 19:16–21) closely echoes Luke’s. Catholics greet her with the angel’s words, “Hail, full of grace,” and honor her as Mother of God.

column4: The Qur’an calls Jesus “a word from Allah” (4:171). The Gospel of John begins: “In the beginning was the Word… and the Word was made flesh.”
Jesus told of a father who runs to meet his returning son. The Church teaches that God is love and that no sin is greater than His mercy.
Christians, Jews and Muslims all look to Abraham. Catholics read Abraham’s offering of his son as a figure of the Father who gave His Son.
The Qur’an says Jesus was not killed or crucified (4:157). Christians hold that he truly died on the Cross and rose on the third day — the heart of the Gospel.
